steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper PlaceNav, which does topological visual navigation by treating subgoal selection as place recognition instead of temporal distance prediction. Explain the background, the problems with current subgoal selection, our idea and its advantages, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Visual navigation and topological navigation
2. How topological navigation systems work; temporal distance prediction
3. Shortcomings of temporal distance prediction
4. PlaceNav: subgoal selection as place recognition
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Visual navigation / topological navigation
- autonomous visual navigation: well-studied in robotics
- topological navigation for known environments: purely vision-based navigation between nodes of a topological map, nodes = images
- advantage: no geometric reconstruction of the environment, no environment-specific control policies

2. Two parts of the system
- subgoal selection: choose map node to reach next
- goal-reaching policy: control commands to take robot to the subgoal
- popular subgoal selection: temporal distance prediction = number of time steps between current camera observation and subgoal candidates
- learning-based, trained on offline datasets of robot trajectories

3. Shortcomings
- impressive real-world navigation in previous works, but two significant shortcomings
- (1) distance estimated individually per candidate -> complexity \mathcal{O}(n) in number of candidate images; needs heuristics to limit candidates; constrains methods for subgoal temporal consistency
- (2) needs robot training data (real or simulated) -> unnecessary data bottleneck; high-quality robotics datasets scarce vs. web-scale data; simulated-data models generalize poorly

4. PlaceNav
- claim: subgoal selection = instance of broader image retrieval
- frame selection as place recognition task
- advantages: large-scale, high-diversity place recognition datasets -> robustness to viewpoint/appearance change; fast nearest-neighbor search over image embeddings -> better scalability, no heuristics (Fig. 1); readily integrates with temporal consistency methods

5. Contributions
- navigation approach decoupling subgoal selection training from robotics datasets (generic place recognition)
- learning-based subgoal selection + Bayesian filter -> temporal consistency
- real-robot demonstrations validating the design
- code and videos on project page

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous visual navigation is a problem that has been studied a lot in robotics. One line of research treats navigation in known environments as topological navigation, which means navigating purely based on vision between the nodes of a topological map, where the nodes are represented by images. The advantage is that this approach does not need a geometric reconstruction of the operating environment and it does not need control policies trained for a specific environment.

A topological navigation system has two parts, subgoal selection and a goal-reaching policy. The subgoal selection module first chooses which map node to reach next, as a subgoal. Then the goal-reaching policy gives the control commands that take the robot to that subgoal. A popular way to do subgoal selection is temporal distance prediction, which means predicting how many time steps there are between the robot's current camera observation and the subgoal candidates. These models are learning-based and they are trained with offline datasets of robot trajectories.

Previous works have shown impressive navigation in the real world, but temporal distance prediction has two big shortcomings. First, the distance must be estimated separately for every subgoal candidate, so the complexity scales at \mathcal{O}(n) with the number of candidate images. Because of this, heuristics are needed to limit the candidates, and the methods that can be used to make subgoals temporally consistent are constrained. Second, temporal distance prediction needs training data that comes from robots, real or simulated, and this is an unnecessary data bottleneck. High-quality robotics datasets are very scarce compared to general web-scale data, and models trained on simulated data have generalization issues.

We claim that subgoal selection is not a unique problem, it is an instance of the broader concept of image retrieval. So we present PlaceNav, which treats subgoal selection as a place recognition task. This design has three advantages. First, there are large-scale and high-diversity datasets for training place recognition models, and these make subgoal selection more robust against changes in viewpoint and appearance. Second, subgoal selection is done by a fast nearest-neighbor search over image embeddings. As illustrated in Fig. 1, this gives better scalability and there is no need for heuristics. Finally, place recognition integrates easily with methods for ensuring temporal consistency.

In summary, our contributions are:

- A navigation approach that decouples the training of subgoal selection models from robotics datasets, by treating subgoal selection as a generic place recognition task.

- Integrating learning-based subgoal selection with a Bayesian filter, which improves temporal consistency.

- Demonstrations with real robots that validate our design experimentally.

Code and videos are on the project page.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous visual navigation is a well-studied problem in robotics [1,2]. One line of research frames navigation in known environments as topological navigation [3,4,5], meaning purely vision-based navigation between nodes of a topological map that are represented by images. The advantage of this approach is that it requires neither a geometric reconstruction of the operating environment [6] nor training environment-specific control policies [7].

Topological navigation systems have two parts: subgoal selection and a goal-reaching policy. First, the subgoal selection module chooses the map node to reach next as a subgoal. Then, the goal-reaching policy produces control commands that take the robot to the selected subgoal. A popular approach to subgoal selection uses temporal distance prediction, which means predicting the number of time steps between the robot's current camera observation and the subgoal candidates [8,9,10,11,12,13]. These learning-based models are trained with offline datasets of robot trajectories.

Previous works have demonstrated impressive real-world navigation [10,12,13], but the temporal distance prediction approach has two significant shortcomings. First, the distance has to be estimated individually for each subgoal candidate, incurring complexity that scales at \mathcal{O}(n) with the number of candidate images. This requires heuristics to limit the candidates and constrains the methods available for ensuring subgoal temporal consistency. Second, temporal distance prediction requires training data that originates from robots, actual or simulated, which introduces an unnecessary data bottleneck. High-quality robotics datasets are very scarce compared to general web-scale data, and models trained with simulated data suffer from generalization issues [14].

We claim that subgoal selection is not a unique problem but an instance of the broader concept of image retrieval. We therefore present PlaceNav, which frames the selection as a place recognition [15] task. This design provides three advantages. First, the large-scale and high-diversity datasets available for training place recognition models make subgoal selection more robust against changes in viewpoint and appearance. Second, subgoal selection is performed by a fast nearest-neighbor search over image embeddings, which, as illustrated in Fig. 1, provides superior scalability and removes the need for heuristics. Finally, place recognition readily integrates with methods for ensuring temporal consistency.

In summary, our contributions are

- A navigation approach that decouples training of subgoal selection models from robotics datasets by treating the selection as a generic place recognition task.

- Integration of learning-based subgoal selection with a Bayesian filter that improves temporal consistency.

- Demonstrations with real robots that experimentally validate our design.

Code and videos are available on the project page.
